stops.name: Yonkers, born on the sixteenth of October
stops.date_confidence: attested: the birth date is corroborated by Wikipedia, the BroadwayWorld obituary of 4 April 2023, and Claudia Bauer's New York Times obituary of 10 April 2023; the city by the NYT, Artdaily, Boston Globe and Prabook obituaries. No hospital, street or attending record survives.
stops.campa: A daughter is born in Yonkers, on the Hudson above the city line, on the sixteenth of October. No hospital, no street and no father's name appear in any record reached; the obituaries that fix the date, written seventy-eight years later, give the city and stop. Her mother teaches and produces theater and dance at the Halsted School in the same town, so dance in this house is a working trade rather than an entertainment. She grows up here and further out in Westchester, a train ride from Manhattan and the professional world in it.
suggested_refs: Claudia Bauer's New York Times obituary of 10 April 2023, which supplies the Yonkers birthplace
sources: Claudia Bauer, New York Times obituary, 10 April 2023 (read via replica edition)

stops.name: The Halsted School, Yonkers: the mother at the front of the room
stops.date_confidence: placement, not a date: the Boston Globe obituary attests that Muller's mother taught and produced theater and dance at the Halsted School in Yonkers, and gives no years at all. 1950 sits inside the childhood by inference only.
stops.campa: The Halsted School is where her mother works, teaching and producing theater and dance for girls in a Yonkers classroom. Everything else about the family is missing; what survives of the woman is one line in an obituary written seventy-eight years later, naming the school and the work and nothing else. A child of that household learns early what a rehearsal actually is: not a performance but the long unglamorous labor before one, counted aloud in a room with the chairs pushed to the wall, repeated until the counting stops being audible.
suggested_refs: Records of the Halsted School, Yonkers, and its theater and dance programme in the 1940s and 1950s

stops.name: Westchester County, pieces made at seven
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: jmtw.org says only 'Creating pieces since age 7' and names no year. Age seven spans 16 October 1951 to 15 October 1952, so the year commonly printed is arithmetic on the birth date, not attestation. Rendered c. 1951-52 and tagged [R].
stops.campa: She begins making dances at seven. The biography she will write herself, decades later, supplies no year for it, no room and no audience, and the only account of the whole beginning sits on a website she controlled. What it describes is not training but authorship: a child who wants less to be taught the steps than to decide what the steps are. The distinction holds for the next sixty years of work, and nothing about the year itself was written down at the time or afterwards. The clause reads: Creating pieces since age 7.
suggested_refs: jmtw.org, official Jennifer Muller biography page, the sole source for the childhood

stops.name: New York, the Pearl Lang Dance Company
stops.date_confidence: the fact is attested (jmtw.org: 'she began dancing professionally at age 15' with Pearl Lang; repeated by BroadwayWorld); the year is reconstruction, since age fifteen runs 16 October 1959 to 15 October 1960. No studio address is recorded, so the canonical New York pin is used.
stops.campa: At fifteen she is a professional. No source names the studio, the wage or the roles she was given, and none says who arranged an audition for a girl that age. The company that hires her belongs to Pearl Lang, who dances lead roles for Martha Graham and carries that technique into a repertory of her own; the first paid work of Muller's life therefore sits inside the Graham line, not the Humphrey and Limón line she will later be counted in. By any ordinary measure she is still a schoolgirl.
suggested_refs: Programs and rosters of the Pearl Lang Dance Company, c. 1959-1963

stops.name: 120 Claremont Avenue, the Juilliard of Morningside Heights
stops.date_confidence: inferred placement: Juilliard occupied 120 Claremont Avenue until its Lincoln Center move of October 1969, so her whole student period is at this building. The entry year is undocumented; 1963 is placed to be consistent with a 1967 degree. An earlier pass wrongly used the Lincoln Center address, and wrongly gave 130 Claremont Avenue, which is the Manhattan School of Music.
stops.campa: Juilliard is still uptown, in a brick building on Claremont Avenue above 122nd Street, years and one move away from the glass at Lincoln Center. She takes her training here, in rooms where the Humphrey and Limón vocabulary is taught as a discipline with a grammar rather than a style with a look. She is already working professionally when she enrolls and will still be working professionally when she leaves. The school vacates the building in October 1969 and the Manhattan School of Music takes it over.

stops.name: Claremont Avenue, the degree and the valedictory
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the valedictory (biographical-directory records giving a 1967 B.S. and class valedictorian; jmtw.org states she completed the degree while a principal dancer). The June date is conventional for commencement and is not documented. No registrar confirmation was obtained.

She has been a principal dancer in a touring company for four years by then, so the degree was assembled in the hours between rehearsal and performance. Her own biography compresses all of it into one clause, that she completed her degree while a principal dancer, and does not mention the valedictory. No registrar record was consulted here; the year and the valedictory come from biographical-directory entries, and the June date is only the usual month for a commencement.

stops.name: New York, entering the José Limón Dance Company
stops.date_confidence: attested: a 1981 New York Times profile and the Limón Dance Company's own posting both state she was 'principal in the Jose Limon Dance Company from 1963 to 1971.' No month is given and no company address is documented, so the canonical New York pin is used.
stops.campa: At eighteen she becomes a principal of the José Limón Dance Company. What she danced there is nowhere written down: no program or cast list from those seasons was located, only the two dates and the word principal. Limón dances Doris Humphrey's line and teaches a body that falls and recovers, weight surrendered to gravity and taken back from it, the opposite of ballet's refusal to admit that weight exists. She spends her twenties dropping and catching herself in front of an audience.

stops.name: New York, the line she stands in
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]: the descent from François Delsarte through Genevieve Stebbins, Ruth St. Denis, Doris Humphrey and José Limón to Muller is the queue's own framing of the lineage, not a claim Muller is recorded making about herself. The 1966 date is a placement inside the Limón years.
stops.campa: The technique she is working in has a pedigree older than any studio teaching it. François Delsarte in Paris built a system for reading feeling off a body; Genevieve Stebbins carried it across the Atlantic and taught it to American women as a practice; from her it passes to Ruth St. Denis, from St. Denis to Doris Humphrey, from Humphrey to Limón, and from Limón into the woman rehearsing his repertory. Muller is not recorded describing herself this way. The chain is drawn by other people, working backwards.
suggested_refs: delsarte.journey.json and stebbins.journey.json for the first two rungs of the descent
sources: QUEUE.md line 913 (the José Limón entry) and line 914 (Muller's own entry)

stops.name: New York, the last Limón season
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (1981 New York Times profile; Limón Dance Company posting). Contradiction flagged and not adjudicated: jmtw.org and the BroadwayWorld obituary both say 'nine years,' while 1963 to 1971 is eight.
stops.campa: She leaves the Limón company in 1971. Her own biography, and every obituary copied from it, calls the tenure nine years; the two sources that give calendar dates give 1963 to 1971, which is eight. Nobody has reconciled the numbers. What is certain is that she entered a founder's company as a teenager and left it in her late twenties, having been for most of a decade the instrument of somebody else's choreography. She had held the second job, the one that ended the first, for three years by then.
suggested_refs: The 1981 New York Times profile giving the 1963-1971 range, cited but not fetched
sources: New York Times profile, 1981 (via search summary)

stops.name: New York, associate artistic director to Louis Falco
stops.date_confidence: attested: Oxford Reference (Oxford Dictionary of Dance) dates her time with Louis Falco's company 1968-74; jmtw.org and Ailey materials give the title Associate Artistic Director and the duration seven years. Contradiction flagged: 1968-74 is six years. No Falco address is documented, so the canonical New York pin is used rather than a coordinate borrowed from another company.
stops.campa: Louis Falco, another dancer out of the Limón company, has a company of his own, and Muller joins it not as a hired body but as associate artistic director. The title matters: it is the first time she is on the making side of the work rather than the executing side. For roughly three years she holds this post and her Limón contract at once, dancing principal roles for one founder while helping shape another's repertory. How two companies divided a single dancer's week is not a question anybody thought to write down.
suggested_refs: Oxford Dictionary of Dance, entry dating the Falco association 1968-74
sources: Oxford Reference, Oxford Dictionary of Dance

stops.name: New York, the Falco years end
stops.date_confidence: attested for the end year (Oxford Reference, 1968-74). The company biography's 'seven years' cannot be squared with that range; both figures are carried and neither is adjudicated.
stops.campa: The Falco association closes in 1974, the same year she founds her own company; the two events are one decision seen from either side. She has by then spent eleven consecutive years inside other people's companies, six of them helping to direct one. The last work she helped him make is named in no source reached. Her own biography counts the Falco period as seven years and the Oxford Dictionary of Dance gives 1968 to 1974, which is six. Both figures are carried here and neither is adjudicated.
suggested_refs: Louis Falco Dance Company records for the seasons 1968 through 1974
sources: Oxford Reference, Oxford Dictionary of Dance

stops.name: New York, Jennifer Muller/The Works is founded
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the city (jmtw.org, Wikipedia, BroadwayWorld). No founding studio, theater or address is recorded anywhere; Wikipedia flags its own article on Muller as a stub.
stops.campa: At twenty-nine she founds Jennifer Muller/The Works, and will be its artistic director for the rest of her life; she never works for another choreographer again. Nothing survives about the founding itself: no studio, no first rehearsal room, no roster of the dancers who turned up. What is documented is what the company later became, in figures the company itself supplies. The encyclopedia article on her runs to a few sentences and flags itself as a stub.

stops.name: New York, Speeds
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year only: jmtw.org dates the work by describing the 2011 grant as staging 'Speeds (1974 work).' No premiere venue, date or cast is recorded in any source reached.
stops.campa: In the founding year she makes Speeds, the piece that will outlive most of the others and still be taught to students four decades later. It is a first work in the plain sense: made by someone with no repertory to be consistent with and nothing yet to protect. Almost nothing about the premiere survives, not the venue, not the date, not the cast; the piece is dated only because a grant application thirty-seven years later calls it a 1974 work. She will look back at it from the far end of the career and say what it was.
stops.quote: 'Speeds' is youthful vibrancy, playfulness and a celebration of life and the body...
stops.quote_source: Jennifer Muller to Bonnie Rosenstock, 'Monte/Muller Move! - No False Moves,' ExploreDance.com, 22 June 2013 (ellipsis in the original)

stops.name: New York, the collaborators
stops.date_confidence: placement, not a record: jmtw.org names Keith Haring, Sandro Chia, Yoko Ono, Keith Jarrett, Burt Alcantara and Marty Beller as collaborators and attaches no dates to any of them; the BroadwayWorld obituary independently names Haring, Ono and Jarrett. 1980 is a placement inside the plausible decade.
stops.campa: She works with painters and musicians and not only with dancers: Keith Haring and Sandro Chia on the visual side, Yoko Ono and Keith Jarrett and the composers Burt Alcantara and Marty Beller on the sound. Her own biography lists them without a single date attached, and the obituary that repeats three of the names adds none, so the record hands over the names and withholds the years. What the list says on its face is plain enough. She made her work with people who were not dancers.
suggested_refs: Programs and designs from the Haring and Chia collaborations, undated in all reachable sources

stops.name: New York, the works given away
stops.date_confidence: placement: jmtw.org states she created commissioned works for 26 repertory companies in nine countries, naming Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, Nederlands Dans Theater and Ballet Contemporáneo among them, with no dates and no work titles. 1985 is a placement, not a documented year.
stops.campa: Twenty-six repertory companies in nine countries take work from her: Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater in New York, Nederlands Dans Theater in the Hague, Ballet Contemporáneo in Buenos Aires, and twenty-three others her biography does not name. No titles are recorded for any of the twenty-six. A commissioned piece leaves the maker's hands in a way a company work does not. It is danced by bodies she did not train, in a house she does not run, and it survives or fails there without her.
suggested_refs: Repertory records of Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, Nederlands Dans Theater and Ballet Contemporáneo for works by Muller

stops.name: The Hague, setting work on Nederlands Dans Theater
stops.date_confidence: inferred [R]: the commission is attested by jmtw.org, but the residency, the year and Muller's presence in the Netherlands are all inferred from the ordinary practice of setting a work on a company. No date, title or record of travel was located.
stops.campa: Nederlands Dans Theater is among the twenty-six. Whether Muller was in the Hague for it, and in what year, is nowhere recorded; the commission is attested and the journey inferred. What the company danced of hers, and whether it kept the piece in repertory, is equally unrecorded. To set a work on a company of that kind is to spend weeks in its studios, teaching a vocabulary to dancers already fluent in others, and then to fly home and let them keep it.
suggested_refs: Nederlands Dans Theater season archives, for the year and title of the Muller commission

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a work for Ballet Contemporáneo
stops.date_confidence: inferred [R] on the same basis as the Hague stop: jmtw.org names Ballet Contemporáneo among the commissioning companies and gives no date, no title and no record of travel. The canonical Buenos Aires pin is used.
stops.campa: Ballet Contemporáneo, the resident modern company of Buenos Aires, commissions her too. Neither the year nor the title of the work is recorded, and no source says whether she made the trip herself. The expressive-movement line that runs from François Delsarte through the Denishawn generation into Limón's studios reaches the southern hemisphere by exactly this route: not by conquest but by invitation, a choreographer flown down to teach a company a way of moving that the company afterwards owns.
suggested_refs: Teatro Municipal General San Martín season records for Ballet Contemporáneo commissions

stops.name: New York, twenty-eight seasons
stops.date_confidence: cumulative figures from jmtw.org, undated and not independently checkable: 28 self-produced New York seasons, tours to 39 countries on four continents and 30 US states, more than 125 works of which seven are full-length. 1999 is a placement at the midpoint of the company's life, not a date in any source.
stops.campa: The arithmetic of running a company: twenty-eight seasons self-produced in New York, thirty-nine countries on four continents, thirty American states, more than a hundred and twenty-five works of which seven are full evenings. Every one of these numbers comes from the company's own accounting and none can be checked against anything else. Behind them is a life spent raising money and booking theaters, and a rate of new work that leaves most of it undocumented anywhere but in her ledger. The ledger is a web page.
suggested_refs: Season programs of Jennifer Muller/The Works, 1974-2023, the underlying record for the company's own totals

stops.name: New York, Women/Create!
stops.date_confidence: the festival is attested by jmtw.org, which names Women/Create! among the company's initiatives and gives no founding year at all. 2005 is a placement.
stops.campa: She founds Women/Create!, a festival that puts women choreographers on a shared bill. It runs alongside the company's own seasons, an act of programming rather than of choreography: the use of a platform she had built for herself to make room for people who had none. Her biography names the festival and gives no founding year, no editions and no participants. The same idea comes back in 2013, when she proposes to a peer that they split a season down the middle instead of competing for one.
suggested_refs: Women/Create! festival programs and participant lists

stops.name: New York, a founding member of the World Arts Council
stops.date_confidence: attested only by jmtw.org, which states she was named a founding member in 2003, the sole American dance-discipline artist among thirty artists chosen across disciplines. No independent record of the council or its founding roster was located; no meeting place is given, so the canonical New York pin is used.
stops.campa: Thirty artists across all disciplines are named founding members of the World Arts Council, and she is the only American from dance among them. Where they met, what the council did and who chose them are absent from the record. The claim exists in one paragraph of her own biography and in every page that copied that paragraph, and nothing was found that contradicts it either. What remains is an honor nobody outside the honoree can verify, with the year 2003 attached to it.
suggested_refs: Founding documents of the World Arts Council, 2003, not located

stops.name: New York, the Muller Polarity Technique
stops.date_confidence: the technique is attested under the name 'Muller Polarity Technique' throughout jmtw.org. Naming discrepancy flagged and not resolved: the atlas brief calls it MULLERWORKS, which is the company's own site name and is applied to the technique by no located source. The 2008 date is a placement; the method has no documented founding date.
stops.campa: The method she teaches has a name of its own, built on Eastern philosophy and on the idea that a body organizes itself between opposed pulls rather than around a single axis. Dances are forgotten faster than ways of standing, so what a choreographer leaves behind that can still be taught is the technique. No founding date for it appears anywhere in the record, and outside listings substitute the company's name for the method's. Her own site never varies the label: Muller Polarity Technique.

stops.name: Berlin, one of seven
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]: jmtw.org states that TanzPlan Berlin's Center for Dance named the Muller Polarity Technique one of seven unique contemporary dance techniques in a published survey. The survey itself was not located; the claim is known only through her own biography and its copies.
stops.campa: A survey published by TanzPlan Berlin's Center for Dance is said to name seven contemporary dance techniques as distinct systems, and hers is one of the seven. That is the whole of what can be said, because the survey has not been found and the claim circulates only through her own biography. If it is accurate, a method assembled in a New York studio was being counted in Berlin among the few that qualify as a technique at all. Which six were the others?

stops.date_confidence: attested by the jmtw.org press page, which lists the article as 'The Muller Technique Introduces East to West' in the September/October 2010 issue. An earlier pass gave the month as September alone. The article text itself was not read.
stops.campa: Education Update runs a piece on her method in an issue dated across September and October, under the title The Muller Technique Introduces East to West. The framing is the one she uses herself: an American vocabulary opened to Eastern philosophy, taught to students who came for modern dance and are handed a cosmology with it. The article itself has not been read here. It is known from one line on her own press page, which gives the title and the issue and nothing of what she said.

stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R], weakly sourced and deliberately not presented at the level of the 2011 grant: the Trophy of Cultural Responsibility for South American contributions appears under 2010 in jmtw.org's self-authored biography and in pages copied from it. No awarding organization, ceremony, place or press notice was locatable.

No body is named as having given it, no ceremony is recorded, and no notice of it exists in any outlet reached. It might have been handed over in Buenos Aires, or in Bogotá, or in a hotel ballroom on Sixth Avenue. The record does not say, and the record here is one line written by the recipient. It sits in the same paragraph as grants that can be traced.

stops.name: The Joyce Theater, the thirty-fifth season
stops.date_confidence: attested by the jmtw.org press page for the month and the venue; the individual performance dates are not given there. An earlier pass pinned the Joyce about 150 metres east of the building; the coordinate here is 175 Eighth Avenue.
stops.campa: Thirty-five years after the founding, the company takes the Joyce for its anniversary season. The Joyce is a converted movie house on Eighth Avenue at Nineteenth Street with something under five hundred seats, the theater a New York modern company aims at once it has outgrown lofts and has not been handed an opera house. She has been running this company longer than most of the dancers on its stage have been alive. The press page that records the season names the month and the venue and no programs.

stops.name: The Joyce Theater, the commission for Bench
stops.date_confidence: attested by jmtw.org: a Joyce Theater commissioning grant, listed elsewhere as the 25@25 programme, for the work Bench. No premiere date, cast or description is given.
stops.campa: The Joyce commissions a new work from her and it becomes Bench. A commissioning grant is a theater betting on a piece that does not exist yet, which at sixty-four means the institution still regards her as somebody with unmade work in her. What Bench is about, who danced it and when it first went up are not stated in any source reached, nor is the shape a bench takes on a stage full of dancers. The company's own listing gives the title, the funder and the year. That is all there is of it.

stops.name: Chelsea Art Museum, Bench in a gallery
stops.date_confidence: attested by the jmtw.org press page for month and venue. The museum stood at 556 West 22nd Street and has since closed; the coordinate is that address. The form the exhibition took is not described.
stops.campa: Bench is exhibited at the Chelsea Art Museum, on West Twenty-Second Street among the galleries. Whether the exhibition was film, installation or live performance is not recorded. A dance shown in a museum is a different object from a dance performed in a theater: it is looked at rather than watched, walked past rather than sat through, and it has to survive an audience that arrives and leaves whenever it likes. The museum closes a few years afterwards.

stops.name: New York, Flowers
stops.date_confidence: attested by the jmtw.org press page for the year alone; no venue, no dates, no description, no cast.
stops.campa: The company performs Flowers in 2010. That sentence is the entire record: a title, a year, a line on a press page, with no venue, no dates, no cast and no description of what the piece did. Of the more than one hundred and twenty-five works she made, most exist exactly this way, as a name attached to a season and danced by people whose names are also gone. The choreography was in bodies and the bodies aged out of it. No tape of this one is in the library collection, which stops at 2005. The paper is what is left.

The students learning it were born a quarter of a century after it was made and are handed a piece of 1974 to carry in their muscles. This is how choreography persists, not on film but by transmission, one body showing another where the weight goes and when to let it drop. Whether she stood in the room in Santa Barbara, or sent a repetiteur in her place, the press page does not say.

She is sixty-six and is being read as a body of work rather than as a working artist, which is a peculiar thing to sit through while still making pieces. The month is April and the year is 2011, and that is the whole of the record.

The category is the whole point of it: a modern dance made in a downtown studio in 1974 is being funded as national heritage, on the same footing as paintings and symphonies, thirty-seven years after it was made. Of everything on her list of honors, this is the one with a paper trail outside her own biography. The grant names the work and its year and treats both as settled.

segments.name: Sanya, and the Season Split in Two

stops.name: Sanya, Hainan: the Spiral Show
stops.date_confidence: attested for month, year and place: the production opened in September 2011 at a Wanda resort venue in Sanya on Hainan Island, produced by Wanda Arts Entertainment Management and directed by Gale Edwards with an all-Chinese cast (Jacksonville.com feature; production materials). An earlier pass placed it in Beijing, wrong by roughly 2,300 kilometres.
stops.campa: She writes and choreographs Spiral for a resort theater in Sanya, at the southern tip of Hainan, some eleven thousand kilometres from the studio where she made Speeds. The cast is entirely Chinese, the director Australian, the producer a property conglomerate assembling an entertainment arm. It is billed as the first Broadway-style musical produced in China, a superlative that comes from the producers and has been repeated ever since without ever being tested against earlier Chinese-language musicals.

stops.name: New York, the season split with Elisa Monte
stops.date_confidence: attested: the jmtw.org press page dates the collaborative programs pairing Muller's work with Elisa Monte and others to a range beginning in 2013 and running to 2017; the earliest year is used. The quote comes from the ExploreDance interview of 22 June 2013.
stops.campa: At sixty-eight she proposes to another choreographer that they stop competing for the same audience and share a bill instead. Elisa Monte agrees. Two companies, one season, the costs and the risk halved and the house doubled: it is an administrative idea before it is an artistic one, and she says so without dressing it up. The paired programs will run in some form for the next four years, billed under both names, with neither company subordinate to the other and neither of them absorbed.
stops.quote: I decided I wanted to do a collaboration to try out a new model for how to put out a season. I approached Elisa, and she decided to join.

stops.name: New York, two women of the same generation
stops.date_confidence: attested: Bonnie Rosenstock, 'Monte/Muller Move! - No False Moves,' ExploreDance.com, 22 June 2013, fetched directly. This interview is the only extended source in Muller's own voice reached for this file.
stops.campa: Asked what she and Monte have in common, she answers as a professional rather than as an aesthete: same generation, same taste for full-bodied movement, and above all the fact that both of them have lasted. Persistence is the quality she names before taste. Two women who ran their own companies for four decades each, toured them internationally, and were both still booking theaters in their sixties. The differences, she adds, are what keeps each of their work her own.
stops.quote: We are two women who come from a similar generation with shared sensibilities. We both like full-bodied movement and have a dancing mentality. We both have lasted and persevered this long in the dance world and have toured a great deal internationally. We also have different approaches that make our work very unique to each of us.
stops.quote_source: Jennifer Muller to Bonnie Rosenstock, 'Monte/Muller Move! - No False Moves,' ExploreDance.com, 22 June 2013
suggested_refs: Bonnie Rosenstock's full ExploreDance interview, 22 June 2013

stops.name: New York, Grass, after Whitman
stops.date_confidence: attested through the ExploreDance interview of 22 June 2013, in which Muller discusses the Whitman-based work Grass. No premiere date, venue or cast for Grass is given in any source reached.
stops.campa: She makes a piece out of Whitman and cannot make it end the way Whitman ends. The material calls for unity, bodies gathered, a celebration; she builds toward it and finds she does not believe it, not that year, not with what she is seeing around her. The work comes out of what she is experiencing whether she recognizes it at the time or not. Grass is danced anyway, without the ending it was designed for. No review of it and no program from it was located, only her account.
stops.quote: I never got to the celebratory moment of it, right? There are years I feel very celebratory, years that I am not, years I'm interested in resolution of conflict, years I am interested in personal transformation. Whether I recognize that or not, the work comes out of what I am experiencing, what I see around me. Walt Whitman does have a sense of celebration, and I thought by the end I could bring the people together and there would be a sense of unity and celebration, but I wasn't feeling it, you know what I mean? I wasn't feeling that our society is in that place, that I could express that right now.
stops.quote_source: Jennifer Muller to Bonnie Rosenstock, 'Monte/Muller Move! - No False Moves,' ExploreDance.com, 22 June 2013
suggested_refs: Walt Whitman, Leaves of Grass, the source text for the work

stops.name: New York, the ending she would not fake
stops.date_confidence: attested: same interview of 22 June 2013, Muller's own account of why the Whitman work's ending was left unresolved. No reviewer's account of the piece was located to set against hers.
stops.campa: The question she is really answering is whether an artist owes an audience relief. She thinks reconciliation matters more than nearly anything, and refuses to stage it before she can feel it, on the grounds that a false ending reads as corn and an audience always knows. The rule has a price attached, and she pays it in the only currency a season has: the piece goes out incomplete by its own design. No reviewer's account was located to set against hers.
stops.quote: I think it's infinitely important to get there, to get over our differences, to understand the tremendous reliance and need for each other. If I did something false at the end, whoopee do-da, we're all together in this, it was going to read corny. I didn't want it to go there.
stops.quote_source: Jennifer Muller to Bonnie Rosenstock, 'Monte/Muller Move! - No False Moves,' ExploreDance.com, 22 June 2013
suggested_refs: Bonnie Rosenstock, ExploreDance.com, 22 June 2013, on the unresolved ending of Grass

stops.name: New York, worlds apart
stops.date_confidence: attested, with a quotation correction: the phrase 'worlds apart' appears in Rosenstock's article as a two-word fragment inside the reporter's own sentence, not as a Muller quotation, and is therefore rendered here as narration. An earlier pass carried it as her direct speech, which it is not.
stops.campa: On the same program sit Speeds, made in 1974, and the new Whitman work. Rosenstock reports her calling the two choreographies worlds apart. One was made by a woman of twenty-nine who had just walked out of eleven years inside other people's companies; the other by a woman of sixty-eight who had spent four decades running her own and could not, that season, find her way to a celebration. Between them lie thirty-nine years of the same person's judgment.
suggested_refs: Bonnie Rosenstock, ExploreDance.com, 22 June 2013, comparing Speeds with the Whitman work

stops.name: Jersey City, the twenty-ninth of March
stops.date_confidence: attested: Claudia Bauer's New York Times obituary of 10 April 2023 ('died on March 29 at her home in Jersey City, N.J.') and the Boston Globe obituary; the date and 'at her home' are corroborated by jmtw.org, Wikipedia and BroadwayWorld, and the cause is reported as natural causes. Earlier passes placed the death in New York City, which is wrong.
stops.campa: She dies at seventy-eight at her home in Jersey City, across the river from the city she worked in for sixty-three years, of natural causes. She is still artistic director of the company she founded; there had been no retirement, no handover, no announced last season. Her own site says she led it for forty-five years and the calendar says forty-nine, and both sentences are in print. The fiftieth anniversary was a year away. Nobody in the notices that follow uses the word retirement.

stops.name: New York, the obituary in the Times
stops.date_confidence: attested: Claudia Bauer, 'Jennifer Muller, Choreographer Whose Dances Told Human Tales, Dies at 78,' The New York Times, 10 April 2023, cited by Wikipedia and read via the newspaper's replica edition, since direct retrieval is blocked.
stops.campa: Twelve days later the Times runs Claudia Bauer's obituary under a headline that names what the work was for: dances that told human tales. Her company's own press language, repeated in every notice that week, calls the company an American Ambassador of Dance and credits the phrase to this same newspaper. No Times article containing it has been found. The epithet appears to have started in the company's materials and to have been attributed backwards ever since.

stops.name: The Joyce Theater, the sixth of November
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Celebration of the Life of Jennifer Muller took place at The Joyce Theater on Monday 6 November 2023 at 7:30 pm, free with RSVP, per Dance Informa, Dance/NYC, The Dance Enthusiast, BroadwayWorld and jmtw.org. An earlier pass gave October 2023, which is wrong.
stops.campa: A celebration of her life is held at the Joyce on a Monday night in November, free to anyone who asks for a seat: remembrances, live performance, and film of work going back decades. The theater is the one that commissioned Bench and housed the thirty-fifth anniversary season, which is as close to a home stage as an independent New York company ever gets. The dancers on the program learned their parts from her, and some of the film shown behind them goes back to the company's first decade.

stops.name: New York, the company continues
stops.date_confidence: attested by the BroadwayWorld artist page: alumni Rosie Lani Fiedelman and Duane Gosa named co-artistic directors and Katy Neely executive director, with the company's 50th anniversary falling in 2024. No month is given for the appointments.
stops.campa: The company does not fold. Two of her own dancers, Rosie Lani Fiedelman and Duane Gosa, take it over as co-artistic directors with Katy Neely as executive director, and it reaches its fiftieth anniversary in 2024. The succession is entirely internal: the people who inherit the repertory are the people who danced it, and a repertory that lives in bodies can be handed on no other way. Nobody is brought in from outside. The name on the door stays hers.

stops.name: Lincoln Center, the Jerome Robbins Dance Division
stops.date_confidence: attested as a catalog description: the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts holds interviews from 1982, 2011 and c. the 1990s, plus VHS and DVD documentation of the company spanning 1976 to 2005. Access is by appointment and the contents were not verified beyond the catalog record. The 2024 date marks the collection as it stands, not an accession.
stops.campa: What is left of the dancing sits on the west side of Lincoln Center, in the Jerome Robbins Dance Division: three interviews, and videotape of the company running from 1976 to 2005. Tape is a poor record of dance and the best one there is; it flattens exactly the weight transfer the whole Humphrey and Limón vocabulary is built on. Access is by appointment. Everything made after 2005, Bench and Spiral and the Whitman piece among it, is not in the collection at all.
